title: Tate residue calculus for a discrete valuation subalgebra
statement:
Let $k\subset K$ be fields and $O\subset K$ a discrete valuation ring [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring] containing $k$, with fraction field $K$ and residue field $\kappa=O/\mathfrak m$ finite over $k$. For every $f\in K$ the quotient $(fO+O)/O$ is finite-dimensional over $k$. Choose a $k$-linear projection $\pi:K\to O$ whose restriction to $O$ is the identity. A $k$-linear endomorphism $T$ of a $k$-vector space $W$ is finite-potent if $T^N(W)$ is finite-dimensional for some integer $N\ge1$; for such $T$, define $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{fp}}(T)$ as the ordinary trace of $T$ on any finite-dimensional $T$-stable subspace of $W$ containing $T^N(W)$, which does not depend on $N$ or on the subspace. For $f,g\in K$ the commutator below is a finite-potent endomorphism of $W=K$. The rule
$$\operatorname{res}_O(f\,dg)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{fp}}\bigl([\pi\circ m_f,m_g]\bigr),\qquad m_f(a)=fa,\quad [A,B]=AB-BA,$$
extends to a $k$-linear map $\Omega^1_{K/k}\to k$ [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials], independent of $\pi$ and of the finite-dimensional subspace in the trace. It annihilates the image of $\Omega^1_{O/k}$ in $\Omega^1_{K/k}$. For a uniformizer $t\in O$ and $u\in O$ it satisfies
$$\operatorname{res}_O(u\,t^{-1}dt)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\kappa/k}(\bar u).$$
If $\kappa/k$ is separable, a $k$-algebra coefficient-field identification $\widehat O\cong\kappa[[t]]$ exists, and for the image $\sum_{m\gg-\infty}a_m t^m dt$ of any $\xi\in\Omega^1_{K/k}$ in continuous differentials of $\kappa((t))/k$ one has
$$\operatorname{res}_O(\xi)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\kappa/k}(a_{-1}).$$

source.place: Tate, §1, pp. 149–151 (finite-potent trace), §2, Theorem 1 and formula (*) p. 152, properties R2 and R4, and §3, Theorem 2 with Theorem 4 (separable residue extension). Blueprint statement: Tate residue and comparison with classical residue.

proof.text: Fix a uniformizer $t$. The DVR definition gives a Noetherian local domain with maximal ideal $(t)$, so the unit-times-uniformizer-power lemma applies. For $f=a/b\ne0$, factoring $a,b\in O\setminus\{0\}$ gives $fO=t^rO$ for an integer $r$. Multiplication by $t^j$ identifies $O/tO=\kappa$ with $t^jO/t^{j+1}O$ for every integer $j$: cancellation proves injectivity, and surjectivity is its displayed description. Thus $t^aO/t^bO$ has $(b-a)[\kappa:k]$ dimensions for $a\le b$, by its finite filtration. Consequently $(fO+O)/O$ is finite-dimensional, including $f=0$.

source.place: §3, p. 154, paragraph preceding Theorem 2 (applied to any DVR with finite residue extension)

proof.text: Use the ideals of the cited operator-ideal theorem with $V=K,A=O$. Step 1 gives $m_f\in E$. Set $F_f=\pi m_f\in E_1$. Since $(\pi-1)fO$ is the image of the finite-dimensional quotient $(O+fO)/O$, $F_f-m_f\in E_2$. More generally, if $F-m_f,G-m_g\in E_2$ and at least one of $F,G$ belongs to $E_1$, then $[F,G]\in E_0$: it belongs to $E_1$ by the ideal property, and modulo $E_2$ it is $[m_f,m_g]=0$. Hence all these commutators are finite-potent. The trace-calculus theorem also establishes the item’s stable-subspace definition of trace for every finite-potent operator, not just these commutators.

The trace of $[F,G]$ is independent of admissible lifts. With $F\in E_1$ fixed, changing $G$ by an element of $E_2$ changes the commutator by an $[E_1,E_2]$ commutator, whose trace is zero. With $G\in E$ fixed and $F,F'\in E_1$ both lifting $f$, $F-F'\in E_0$ and the change has trace zero by $[E_0,E]$. All additions are within $E_0$, where trace is linear. Interchanging the two arguments handles the case in which only the second lift lies in $E_1$. In particular $\beta(f,g)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{fp}}[F_f,F_g]$ equals $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{fp}}[\pi m_f,m_g]$; changing $\pi$ does not change it. Linearity of the chosen lifts and of trace on $E_0$ makes $\beta$ $k$-bilinear; $\beta(f,c)=0$ for $c\in k$ by choosing $G=c\,1$.

For $f,g,h\in K$, let $F,G,H\in E_1$ lift their multiplications modulo $E_2$. The products $GH,FG,FH$ lift $gh,fg,fh$, because $E_2$ is an ideal of $E$. The operator identity
$$[F,GH]-[FG,H]-[FH,G]=[G,[F,H]]$$
has right side of trace zero: $[F,H]\in E_0$ and $G\in E$. Taking traces and using the lift independence gives $\beta(f,gh)=\beta(fg,h)+\beta(fh,g)$. The presentation of Kähler differentials in the cited definition now gives a unique $k$-linear map with $f\,dg\mapsto\beta(f,g)$: additivity and $k$-constants follow from Step 3, and the displayed identity kills precisely the Leibniz relations, also after multiplication by any $f$. This is the required residue map, independent of the projection and trace subspace.

source.place: §2, Theorem 1, descent through the presentation of differentials

proof.text:
Here is the finite calculation that will also control completion. For nonzero $f,g$ put $T=[\pi m_f,m_g]$, $B=O+gO$ and $C=B\cap f^{-1}O\cap(fg)^{-1}O$. Both $B,C$ are fractional ideals $t^bO,t^cO$, and Step 1 makes $B/C$ finite-dimensional. One has $T(K)\subset B$, and for $x\in C$, $fx,fgx\in O$, whence $T(x)=fgx-gfx=0$. Apply trace additivity first to $B\subset K$ and then to $C\subset B$. The induced operator on $K/B$ and the restriction to $C$ are zero, so
$$\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{fp},K}(T)=\operatorname{Tr}_k(T\mid B/C).$$
The case $f=0$ or $g=0$ gives zero directly. If $f,g\in O$, then $B=C=O$, so $\operatorname{res}_O(f\,dg)=0$. Every regular differential is a sum of such terms by the presentation of $\Omega^1_{O/k}$, proving annihilation of its image.

For $u\in O$, take $T=[\pi m_{u/t},m_t]$. Its image is contained in $O$, and for $x\in tO$, $T(x)=ux-t\pi(ux/t)=0$. For $x\in O$, reduction of $T(x)=ux-t\pi(ux/t)$ modulo $tO$ is $\bar u\bar x$. Thus the same two invariant-subspace trace decompositions as Step 5 give $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{fp}}T=\operatorname{Tr}_k(m_{\bar u}\mid O/tO)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\kappa/k}(\bar u)$. This works for inseparable $\kappa/k$ too; no coefficient field has been used.

source.place: §2, R4, specialized to g=t and h=u

proof.text: Put $R=\widehat O=\varprojlim O/t^nO$. The cited completion lemmas give completeness for $tR$ and $R/t^nR=O/t^nO$, compatibly with the canonical maps. This makes $R$ local with maximal ideal $tR$: an element whose residue is nonzero has an inverse modulo every $t^n$ (lift the residue inverse and use a finite geometric sum for the nilpotent error); uniqueness makes the inverses compatible. Multiplication by $t$ on $R$ is injective: if $tx=0$, its coordinate $x_{n+1}$ is in $t^nO/t^{n+1}O$ by cancellation in $O$, so $x_n=0$ for all $n$. Also $O\to R$ is injective, since a nonzero $ut^r$ is not in $t^{r+1}O$. Completeness and the complete-pair lemma make the local ring $R$ henselian. If $\kappa/k$ is separable, apply the cited residue-section lemma to $k,\kappa,R$ with the empty separating family (so its generated subfield is $k$). It gives a $k$-algebra section $s:\kappa\to R$ of reduction.

source.place: Completion and separable coefficient section: Stacks 05GG, 0ALJ, followed by the existing henselian separably generated residue-section tool

proof.text: With this section, define $\kappa[[T]]\to R$ by $\sum a_iT^i\mapsto\sum s(a_i)t^i$, where the sum means its compatible finite truncations. Completeness makes it defined, and finite multiplication modulo each $t^n$ proves it is a $k$-algebra map. It is onto: successively subtract the residue lift and divide by $t$ to obtain all coefficients. It is injective: the first nonzero coefficient, after cancellation of its power of $t$, has nonzero residue. Thus $R\cong\kappa[[t]]$, identifying $t$ with $T$. Inverting $t$ identifies $R[1/t]$ with $\kappa((t))$; this is a field, since a nonzero series is a power of $t$ times a series with invertible constant term, whose inverse is obtained recursively. The injection $O\to R$ extends to $K\hookrightarrow\kappa((t))$. Moreover $K\cap R=O$: a fraction $ut^r$ with $r<0$ cannot belong to $R$, by reduction modulo $t$.

source.place: Coefficient-field power-series coordinates: explicit successive-residue construction supplementing Tate §3, Theorem 2

proof.text: The finite quotient in Step 5 proves that residue is preserved by $K\hookrightarrow\widehat K=\kappa((t))$. Indeed $\widehat K=K+R$: any finite principal part can be lifted from $O/t^nO$. Extend $\pi$ to a projection $\widehat\pi:\widehat K\to R$ by $\widehat\pi(x+a)=\pi(x)+a$ for $x\in K,a\in R$; the intersection equality of Step 8 makes this well-defined. For the fixed $f,g\in K$, the completed $\widehat B=R+gR$ and $\widehat C=\widehat B\cap f^{-1}R\cap(fg)^{-1}R$ have the same exponents $b,c$ as $B,C$. The quotient identifications modulo powers give $B/C\cong\widehat B/\widehat C$. Since $\widehat\pi|_K=\pi$, this isomorphism intertwines the induced commutators. Step 5 on both fields therefore equates their traces, with no continuity assertion about the arbitrary original $\pi$.

source.place: §2, Remark formula (*), applied to completion; §3, definition of local residue

proof.text:
Compute now on $\widehat K$ with the projection $P$ taking the nonnegative powers of $t$. Let $f=\sum_{i\ge p}a_it^i$, $g=\sum_{j\ge q}b_jt^j$. For a coordinate $zt^r$, the coefficient of $t^r$ in $[Pm_f,m_g](zt^r)$ is
$$z\sum_{i+j=0}a_ib_j\bigl(1_{r\ge0}-1_{r+i\ge0}\bigr).$$
There are only finitely many contributing pairs, since $p\le i\le-q$. Compute the ordinary trace on $B/C=t^bR/t^cR$ from Step 5 using a $k$-basis of $\kappa$ in each degree. Its diagonal block in degree $r$ is multiplication by the displayed sum. Terms outside this finite strip have zero diagonal, since the operator has image in $B$ and kills $C$. For each fixed $i$, summing $1_{r\ge0}-1_{r+i\ge0}$ over $r\in\mathbf Z$ gives $-i=j$ (count the finite interval between $0$ and $-i$, with its sign). Consequently
$$\operatorname{res}_R(f\,dg)=\sum_{i+j=0}j\operatorname{Tr}_{\kappa/k}(a_ib_j)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\kappa/k}([t^{-1}]f(t)g'(t)).$$
This is a finite quotient matrix calculation even when the series have infinitely many positive terms, so no passage of a trace through an infinite sum is used.

source.place: §3, Theorem 2, coefficient calculation; §2, formula (*) (expanded to finite separable coefficient fields)

proof.text: The canonical continuous differential of a Laurent series is $g\mapsto g'(t)dt$, with the coefficients differentiated as zero. This is a $k$-derivation: coefficients of products are finite convolution sums and satisfy the termwise product rule. Separability makes this the usual continuous differential over $k$: for $a\in\kappa$ its separable minimal polynomial gives $0=P'(a)da$, hence $da=0$, and continuity then differentiates a power series term by term. The presentation of differentials sends $f\,dg$ to $fg'(t)dt$. Every $\xi\in\Omega^1_{K/k}$ is a finite sum of such generators. Combining Steps 9 and 10 and linearity gives $\operatorname{res}_O(\xi)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\kappa/k}(a_{-1})$ for its continuous Laurent differential. Since the left side was already constructed without coordinates, this comparison applies to every coefficient-field identification and uniformizer as stated.

split_report.blueprint: Statement of sk-thm-picard-duality: Tate’s k-linear residue at a closed point, its annihilation of regular differentials and comparison with the classical residue when the residue extension is separable.

tool_uses.why: Generic DVR factorization is needed to bound fractional ideals; the unit has no separate algebraic factorization lemma.
Generic finite-generated-ideal completion theorem supplies completeness and the residue quotient for the coefficient-field construction.
Canonical quotient identifications control the finite trace calculation after completion.
Completeness implies henselianity, needed solely for constructing a separable coefficient section.
Its empty separating-family case constructs the k-compatible finite separable residue-field section; no lemma in this unit gives this generic tool.

Status: the item is unsplit on live and side-live, there is no repair note, and it is not on the dropped list. The statement is unchanged. Steps 1–11 are correct. Lifts F_f = πm_f lie in E₁ and differ from m_f by an element of E₂, because (π−1)fO is the image of (fO+O)/O. Lift independence uses the two commutator clauses of the ideals node. The Leibniz operator identity expands to [G,[F,H]], which has zero trace; Tate p.152 wrongly writes it as 0, and the delivery handles this correctly. The finite quotient B/C is Tate's (*). For u∈O, u t⁻¹dt has residue Tr_{κ/k}(ū) with positive sign, consistent with R4; no separability is used. Completion steps: R is complete and local, hence henselian. The residue-section lemma with the empty family gives the coefficient field. R≅κ[[t]] and K∩R=O. π̂ is well defined on K̂=K+R, and B/C≅B̂/Ĉ. I recomputed the Laurent strip: the diagonal coefficient is Σ_{i+j=0}a_ib_j(1_{r≥0}−1_{r+i≥0}), the sum over r is −i=j, and the result Tr([t⁻¹]fg′) holds in every characteristic. Both new nodes are true, self-contained, statement-only and not duplicates (rg -L over the DAG), and neither restates the item; I checked edge cases A=0, A=V and the cyclicity proof.
